intro:
These exercises move from the highest-level decision in an MPI program down to the units a collective actually consumes. You start by choosing a partition and a collective shape from the algorithm, then learn to spot the layout mistake (Vec<Vec<T>>) that quietly makes every scatter and gather harder, then implement and test the balanced block-partition helper that every rank runs before it touches data. The later exercises shift from correctness to operations: converting row thinking into the cell counts and displacements a collective expects, building a measurement plan that separates compute from communication, and committing to a hybrid MPI-plus-threads deployment shape with an honest core budget.

The through-line is the chapter's central claim: an MPI program has two stacked boundaries with different rules. The outer boundary between ranks is full processes with separate address spaces, where nothing is shared and everything must be copied as a flat contiguous payload. The inner boundary inside a rank is ordinary Rust threading, where Arc<T> and Send/Sync still govern shared immutable state. Almost every hard MPI bug is one wrong boundary: the wrong layout, the wrong unit at a collective, one rank doing more work, or one node running too many local threads against too few cores.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose process partitioning and collective shape from the algorithm
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Partition by rows first. The workload is described as a row-wise dense pass, which means each output row is computed from data that lives contiguously in a row-major buffer. A row partition makes each rank's share a single contiguous slice (start_row * cols .. end_row * cols), so the local kernel walks memory in the same order the algorithm reads it, and the eventual scatter or gather operates on one contiguous region per rank with no gather-list gymnastics. Column partitioning would force each rank to touch strided slices of every row, fighting the row-major layout and the cache. Tiling is a real option for two-dimensional stencils where a rank needs neighbors on all four sides, but it only pays for itself once the access pattern is genuinely 2D and halo exchange dominates; for a plain row-wise pass it adds boundary bookkeeping you do not need. The honest first move is the simplest layout that matches the access pattern, which here is balanced blocks of rows.

For the single global convergence scalar, the collective that fits depends entirely on who needs the answer. If only rank 0 needs the scalar (for example, to log it or decide termination centrally), MPI_Reduce is the honest fit: it combines one value per rank into a single result delivered to the root, and the non-root ranks contribute but do not receive. If every rank needs the scalar to drive its own next iteration, that is MPI_Allreduce: the same reduction, but the combined result is delivered to every rank. The third prompt is exactly this distinction made concrete. In an iterative solver where each rank decides locally whether to continue or to scale its next step using the global residual, allreduce is correct, because a reduce would leave every non-root rank without the number it needs, forcing an extra broadcast that allreduce already folds into one optimized collective. The right framing is not the API name but the data-flow shape: reduce is a funnel to one rank, allreduce is a funnel followed by a fan-out to all, and you pick based on the synchronization the next iteration actually requires.
criteria: Chooses row partitioning and justifies it from the row-major, row-wise access pattern rather than by preference.
Distinguishes reduce (result to root only) from allreduce (result to every rank) by who consumes the scalar.
Frames the choice in layout and synchronization terms: contiguous slices and funnel-versus-funnel-plus-fanout, not just API names.

exerciseSolutions.title: Find the Vec<Vec<T>> mistake before the collective boundary
exerciseSolutions.solution:
A Vec<Vec<f64>> for a dense matrix is the wrong default precisely at the collective boundary. The outer Vec holds rows pointers; each inner Vec is a separate heap allocation with its own length, capacity, and data pointer. So a dense R-by-C matrix becomes R+1 allocations instead of one, and reading element (r, c) is a double indirection: load the row pointer, then load the cell. The rows are not contiguous with one another, so the matrix has no single base pointer and no single length that describes the whole payload. That is the real problem, because an MPI send or a scatter is described by exactly those two things: a starting pointer and an element count over a contiguous region. With nested storage there is no contiguous region spanning multiple rows, so before you can scatter you must pack every row block into a temporary flat buffer, and after you gather you must unpack back into freshly allocated inner Vecs. The nested shape forces a copy on both sides of every collective, plus the per-row allocation churn, and it throws away cache locality during the local kernel as well.

One flat Vec<f64> of length rows * cols, indexed as matrix[row * cols + col], fixes all of this. The whole matrix is one allocation with one base pointer and one length, so a rank's row block start_row..end_row maps directly to the contiguous slice matrix[start_row * cols .. end_row * cols] that a scatter can hand out and a gather can write back with no packing step. You carry the shape separately as explicit row counts (and the cols multiplier), which is cheap and keeps the buffer itself a pure payload. This is the chapter's rule that flat buffers win in MPI: contiguous storage satisfies the caches, the local kernel, and the FFI boundary into the system MPI library all at once. The nested shape is still the honest choice when the data is genuinely ragged: rows of different lengths (a jagged adjacency list, variable-length records, a sparse structure where each row stores only its nonzeros). There, a flat buffer would need its own counts-and-offsets table to describe the ragged structure anyway, and per-row ownership accurately models data that really does have per-row lengths. The decision is dense versus ragged, not pretty syntax versus ugly syntax.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Dense data wants one flat buffer; nested Vec<Vec<T>> is only honest when rows are truly ragged.
criteria: Explains the dense cost precisely: R+1 allocations, double indirection, and no single contiguous region for a collective.
Recommends one flat Vec<f64> indexed as row * cols + col, tied to scatter/gather operating on a contiguous slice.
Names ragged data (jagged/sparse rows of differing lengths) as the case where nested per-row ownership is correct.

exerciseSolutions.title: Implement a balanced block partition for matrix rows
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The helper must split rows as evenly as possible and hand any remainder rows to the lowest ranks, returning a half-open [start_row, end_row) range. The clean formula is the one from the chapter's first example. Let base = rows / ranks be the floor share every rank gets, and remainder = rows % ranks be the number of rows left over. Each of the first `remainder` ranks takes one extra row. A rank's length is therefore base + 1 if rank < remainder, else base, which Rust writes branch-free as base + usize::from(rank < remainder). The start offset must account for the extra rows already handed out to lower ranks: rank * base places the floor shares, and rank.min(remainder) adds exactly one for each earlier rank that received an extra row (capped at remainder, since once the remainder is exhausted no further extras exist). The end is start + len, kept exclusive so adjacent ranks meet without overlap and the union of all ranges is exactly 0..rows.

Using one formula for every rank, including rank 0, is the point of the exercise. Special-casing rank 0 and hoping the rest line up is how off-by-one gaps and overlaps appear: the invariant you want is that block_range(rows, ranks, r).end_row == block_range(rows, ranks, r + 1).start_row for every adjacent pair, which a single closed-form expression guarantees by construction. Verifying the rank-2 cell count for rows = 11, ranks = 4, cols = 5: base = 2, remainder = 3, so ranks 0, 1, 2 each get 3 rows and rank 3 gets 2, giving ranges 0..3, 3..6, 6..9, 9..11. Rank 2 owns rows 6..9, which is 3 rows, and 3 * 5 = 15 cells. That is the value the lab prints.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: One closed-form expression for all ranks; remainder rows go to the lowest ranks, ranges stay half-open and contiguous.
criteria: Remainder rows go to the lowest ranks via base + usize::from(rank < remainder), with start offset rank * base + rank.min(remainder).
Every range is half-open and adjacent ranges meet exactly, so the partition is non-overlapping and covers 0..rows.
Reproduces the lab output: ranges 0..3, 3..6, 6..9, 9..11 and rank-2 cell count 3 * 5 = 15.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose flat counts and displacements for a collective
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is a unit mismatch at the collective boundary. The inherited code computes row counts correctly, but a scatter or gather over a row-major f64 buffer is described in elements (cells), not in rows. Passing row displacements where the collective expects element displacements means every rank after rank 0 reads or writes its slice cols-times too close to the buffer start, corrupting overlapping regions. The conversion from rows to cells must happen exactly once, at the point where you build the displacement and count tables the collective consumes, by multiplying the row quantities by cols. Keep two clearly named tables: the counts table stays in the unit the algorithm reasons in (rows) for the load-balancing logic, and a parallel send-counts/displacements pair is derived in cells right before the call. The chapter states the arithmetic as one rule: a cell's position is row * cols + col, so a row range maps to a cell range by multiplying both ends by cols.

Cumulative displacements follow from a single forward walk over the counts. The displacement of rank 0 is 0; the displacement of rank k is the sum of all earlier ranks' element counts, so you accumulate an offset as you go: out.push(offset); offset += rows_for_rank * cols. This is exactly displacements_in_cells from the chapter's second example. The invariant is that displacement[k] + send_count_in_cells[k] == displacement[k+1] for every k, and displacement[last] + send_count[last] == rows * cols, so the offsets tile the whole buffer with no gaps or overlaps. The test that catches this before a full cluster run is a tiny uneven matrix with hand-computed slices. Take rows = 5, cols = 2, ranks = 2: row_counts is [3, 2], so send counts in cells are [6, 4] and displacements in cells are [0, 6]. Assert those three vectors exactly, and assert that the reconstructed slices recover the original buffer. The unevenness is what makes the test sharp: a divisible shape can pass even with the rows-versus-cells bug masked, but an uneven shape with known offsets fails loudly the moment the units are wrong.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Counts stay in rows for load logic; the rows-to-cells conversion happens once when building send counts and displacements.
criteria: Converts to the collective's unit (cells = rows * cols) exactly once, at the point the count/displacement tables are built.
States the cumulative rule: displacement[k] is the running sum of earlier ranks' cell counts via a single forward walk.
Proposes a focused test: a tiny uneven matrix (5x2 over 2 ranks) with hand-computed counts [6,4] and displacements [0,6].

exerciseSolutions.title: Profile communication-heavy HPC work conceptually before rewriting it
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Resist the single-process instinct to profile the arithmetic kernel first. The kernel code path is unchanged and the mesh change is the only new variable, so the most likely cause is a shift in partition shape or communication pattern, not arithmetic intensity. The measurement plan separates time into three buckets per rank, every iteration: local compute time (the kernel between communication calls), halo-exchange time (the neighbor sends and receives), and collective time (the convergence allreduce or reduce). You place explicit timers around each region using a monotonic clock, accumulate per-region totals per rank, and crucially record them per rank rather than only on rank 0, because rank 0 is frequently not the bottleneck and any single-rank summary hides the slowest participant. The chapter's framing is the right question: who is waiting for whom, and where.

To distinguish load imbalance from too-frequent communication, look at two different signals. The rank-local signal is the spread of local compute time across ranks: compute the min, max, and the gap between the slowest and fastest rank's kernel time. A large spread means imbalance, which a mesh change easily causes by leaving one rank with more cells or more boundary work even though every rank runs identical code. The cross-rank signal is the time ranks spend blocked inside collectives: because a collective does not complete until the slowest rank arrives, time attributed to the allreduce is mostly wait time imposed by imbalance elsewhere, not the cost of the reduction itself. So a high collective-wait number with a wide compute spread points at imbalance; a high collective count with small per-call payloads and a narrow compute spread points at communication that is simply too frequent (for example, a barrier or allreduce inside a loop that could be hoisted or batched). Log per rank: local compute time, halo time, collective wait time, message counts and sizes, and the local cell or element count so imbalance is visible as a number rather than inferred. Only after that story is clear does kernel micro-optimization make sense; optimizing arithmetic while ranks are idle in an allreduce moves no real time.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Three per-rank timer buckets plus the local cell count make imbalance and chatty collectives distinguishable from kernel cost.
criteria: Separates compute, communication (halo), and collective wait time with explicit per-region timers.
Names a rank-local signal (spread of local compute time / local cell count) and a cross-rank signal (collective wait time).
Defers kernel micro-optimization until the communication and imbalance story is established.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose hybrid MPI plus threads and cluster deployment policy deliberately
exerciseSolutions.solution:
I would deploy one rank per socket (or per NUMA domain) with a per-rank thread pool sized to the cores that rank owns, which is the chapter's dominant production layout, not one rank per core. The reasoning is economic and topological: crossing the network is the expensive boundary, so you want as few ranks as the topology allows while still keeping each rank's memory traffic inside one NUMA domain. CPU-heavy kernels parallelize well across cores within a socket using a Rayon or plain thread pool, and the single read-mostly lookup table per rank is loaded once per process and shared by all of that rank's threads, so more threads per rank amortizes both the table's memory footprint and the network cost. Pure one-rank-per-core would replicate the lookup table N times per socket and multiply the number of participants in every collective, inflating both memory and synchronization cost. A balanced mix only makes sense if a single socket spans multiple NUMA domains, in which case one rank per NUMA domain keeps each rank's allocations local.

Inside a rank, the boundaries map cleanly. The CPU-heavy kernel over the rank's row block is the intra-rank parallel work: a Rayon parallel iterator over the local rows, or a fixed thread pool, with no MPI calls inside the pool. The read-mostly lookup table is shared immutable state, so it lives behind an Arc<T> (Arc<LookupTable>) cloned into each worker; it is read concurrently, never mutated during compute, so Arc plus shared &T references satisfy Send and Sync without any lock. Arc and threads stay strictly inside the rank: Rust's thread rules govern that inner boundary, and an Arc never crosses a process boundary because it is a pointer into one address space that means nothing in another. MPI remains the only inter-rank boundary, carrying flat typed buffers: scatter the block in, allreduce the convergence scalar across ranks, and write the checkpoint. The load block -> local compute -> allreduce -> checkpoint pipeline therefore has exactly one shared-memory region (per rank) and one message-passing region (across ranks), and they never blur.

The core-budget tradeoff is the failure mode to police. A hybrid design is only good if ranks_per_node * threads_per_rank stays at or below the cores the scheduler granted per node; oversubscription makes threads contend for cores, and because a collective waits for the slowest rank, one oversubscribed node drags the entire job. Before rollout I would require at least these observability hooks: (1) CPU oversubscription per node (runnable threads versus allocated cores, e.g. load average against core count), (2) collective wait time per rank, which exposes imbalance hiding as communication cost, (3) per-rank throughput (cells per second) to surface a straggler rank, and (4) thread-pool queue depth inside each rank to detect intra-rank saturation. With those four, the tight cores-per-node policy is enforceable as numbers rather than as hope, and a misconfigured rank-by-thread fan-out shows up before it silently halves cluster throughput.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: One rank per socket; Arc-shared lookup table and a thread pool stay intra-rank; MPI carries only flat buffers across ranks.
criteria: Commits to one-rank-per-socket (or per-NUMA) hybrid with reasoning tied to network cost, NUMA locality, and CPU-heavy kernels.
Cleanly separates intra-rank shared immutable state (Arc<LookupTable>, thread pool) from the inter-rank MPI boundary carrying flat buffers.
Names at least three observability hooks: CPU oversubscription, collective wait time, per-rank throughput, and thread-pool queue depth.
Polices the core budget: ranks_per_node * threads_per_rank <= cores_per_node so one oversubscribed node cannot stall the collective.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
rank 0 = 0..3
rank 1 = 3..6
rank 2 = 6..9
rank 3 = 9..11
cells rank2 = 15
labSolution.explanation:
The lab completes the starter by replacing the naive block_range (which used a single rows / ranks share and left the remainder stranded on a phantom range) with the balanced formula. With rows = 11 and ranks = 4, base = 11 / 4 = 2 and remainder = 11 % 4 = 3. Ranks 0, 1, and 2 are each below the remainder threshold, so they take base + 1 = 3 rows; rank 3 takes base = 2 rows. The start offset rank * base + rank.min(remainder) accounts for the extra rows already handed to lower ranks, producing the contiguous half-open ranges 0..3, 3..6, 6..9, and 9..11.

Because every range is half-open and the start of each rank equals the end of the previous one, the four blocks tile 0..11 exactly with no overlap and no stranded rows, which is the property a real scatter relies on. The final line converts rank 2's row range into a cell count: rank 2 owns 3 rows, and at cols = 5 that is 3 * 5 = 15 cells, matching the chapter's rule that a row range maps to a cell range by multiplying by cols. The program uses only the standard library and prints the five expected lines.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is MPI primarily a process model rather than a shared-memory model?
reviewAnswers.answer: MPI runs each rank as a full operating-system process with its own private address space, typically spread across separate machines on a cluster, so there is no shared memory for ranks to read or write. Nothing is implicitly shared between ranks; every byte one rank needs from another must be copied explicitly as a message. This is the outer of the two boundaries in an MPI program, and it is exactly why partitioned data must be packed into flat contiguous buffers rather than shared through pointers. Shared-memory parallelism (threads, Arc, locks) still exists, but only inside a single rank, never across the rank boundary.

reviewAnswers.question: Why do flat contiguous buffers simplify collective operations so much?
reviewAnswers.answer: A collective like scatter, gather, reduce, or allreduce describes its payload as a starting pointer plus an element count over a contiguous region, and the same is true of the caches and the FFI boundary into the system MPI library. A flat row-major Vec<f64> is one allocation with one base pointer and one length, so a rank's row block is already the contiguous slice the collective expects, with no packing or unpacking step. A nested Vec<Vec<f64>> has no single contiguous region spanning rows, so it forces a copy into a temporary flat buffer before every send and back again after every receive. Flat layout satisfies the kernel, the cache, and the collective simultaneously.

reviewAnswers.question: What is the practical difference between reduce and allreduce in an iterative solver?
reviewAnswers.answer: Both combine one value per rank (a sum, max, and so on) into a single result, but they differ in who receives it. Reduce delivers the combined result only to the root rank, while allreduce delivers it to every rank. In an iterative solver where each rank needs the global convergence residual to decide whether to continue or how to scale its next step, allreduce is correct because every rank needs the number; using reduce would leave non-root ranks without it and force a separate broadcast that allreduce already folds into one optimized collective. Use reduce only when a single rank consumes the aggregate, for example to log it or make a central termination decision.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is a balanced partition helper worth testing as a first-class component?
reviewAnswers.answer: Every rank runs the partition math before it touches any data, and its correctness underpins every subsequent scatter, gather, and slice index, so a single off-by-one there corrupts the whole run. The hard requirement is that ranges are half-open, non-overlapping, and cover 0..rows exactly even when the row count is not divisible by the rank count, which is precisely where ad hoc per-rank branching introduces gaps or overlaps. Because it is a small pure function of (rows, ranks, rank), it is cheap to unit-test with uneven shapes and known expected ranges. Testing it as a first-class component catches the most common distribution bug locally, before it manifests as silent data corruption on a full cluster.

reviewAnswers.question: What signals tell you an MPI program is communication-bound instead of compute-bound?
reviewAnswers.answer: Time spent blocked inside collectives is the primary signal: a collective is a barrier that does not complete until the slowest rank arrives, so a profiler showing ranks idle in an allreduce usually indicates communication or imbalance cost, not arithmetic. A wide spread between the slowest and fastest rank's local compute time points to load imbalance (one rank doing more work), while a high count of small collectives with a narrow compute spread points to communication that is simply too frequent, such as a barrier or allreduce inside a hot loop. You separate these by placing per-region timers around compute, halo exchange, and collectives, recorded per rank rather than only on rank 0. If collective wait time and halo time dominate the kernel time, the program is communication-bound.

reviewAnswers.question: Why can hybrid MPI plus threads become slower if you ignore total core budgeting on the node?
reviewAnswers.answer: In a hybrid layout each node runs ranks_per_node times threads_per_rank software threads; if that product exceeds the cores the scheduler allocated per node, the threads oversubscribe the cores and contend for CPU time instead of running in parallel. Because every collective waits for the slowest rank, a single oversubscribed node where threads are time-slicing drags the entire job's pace, not just its own. The speedup you expected from more threads is consumed by context-switching and scheduling overhead. Keeping ranks_per_node times threads_per_rank at or below cores_per_node, and monitoring CPU oversubscription per node, is what keeps the hybrid design honest.
